Ali Bongo is a diplomat. A member of the Gabonese Democratic Party, Bongo is the son of Omar Bongo, who was president from 1967 until his death in 2009.
In what year was Prince George of Wales born?
Prince George of Wales (George Alexander Louis; born 22 July 2013) is a member of the British royal family.
In what year was Alexander Lukashenko born?
Alexander Lukashenko: In 1990, Lukashenko was elected to the Supreme Soviet of the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic.
In what year was Vajiralongkorn born?
Vajiralongkorn (born 28 July 1952), also known by his regnal name Rama X, is King of Thailand, reigning since 2016.
In what year was Queen Victoria born?
Queen Victoria: Victoria was the daughter of Prince Edward, Duke of Kent and Strathearn (the fourth son of King George III), and Princess Victoria of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld.
In what year did Edward VII die?
Edward VII: As Prince of Wales, Edward travelled throughout Britain performing ceremonial public duties and represented Britain on visits abroad.
In what year did Edward VIII die?
Edward VIII: Edward was born during the reign of his great-grandmother Queen Victoria as the eldest child of the Duke and Duchess of York, later King George V and Queen Mary.
In what year was Palestinian Islamic Jihad founded?
Palestinian Islamic Jihad: PIJ formed as an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood and was influenced ideologically in its formation by the Islamic Revolution in Iran.
In what year was Kingdom of Israel (Samaria) founded?
Kingdom of Israel (Samaria): Its beginnings date back to the first half of the 10th century BCE.
In what year was Lutheranism founded?

House of Orange-Nassau: William the Silent. Several members of the house served during the Eighty Years' War and after as stadtholder ("governor"; Dutch: stadhouder) during the Dutch Republic.
Kuomintang: Sun Yat-sen. The Kuomintang (KMT) is a major political party in the Republic of China (Taiwan).
East India Company: John Watts. The East India Company (EIC) was an English, and later British, joint-stock company that was founded in 1600 and dissolved in 1874.
In which country is Fall of Kabul (2021)?
Fall of Kabul (2021): Afghanistan. On 15 August 2021, Afghanistan's capital city of Kabul was captured by the Taliban after a major insurgent offensive that began in May 2021.
In which country is Free Cause Party based?
Free Cause Party: Turkey. The Free Cause Party (Turkish: Hür Dava Partisi, HÜDA PAR; Kurdish: Partiya Doza Azad) is a Kurdish Sunni Islamist political party in Turkey.
In which country did the Battle of Kiev (1941) take place?
Battle of Kiev (1941): Ukraine. The battle lasted from 7 July to 26 September 1941 as part of Operation Barbarossa, the Axis invasion of the Soviet Union.
In which country did the Easter Rising take place?

Easter Rising: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The Easter Rising (Irish: Éirí Amach na Cásca), also known as the Easter Rebellion, was an armed insurrection in Ireland during Easter Week in April 1916.
In which country is Janata Party based?
Janata Party: India. The Janata Party (JP, lit. 'People's Party') is an unrecognised political party in India.
In which country did the Battle of the Pyramids take place?
Battle of the Pyramids: Egypt. Occurring near the village of Embabeh, Ottoman Egypt, the battle was named by Napoleon after the distant Great Pyramid of Giza.
Babylonia: Iraq. It emerged as an Akkadian-populated but Amorite-ruled state c. 1894 BC.
In which country is Finns Party based?
Finns Party: Finland. It was founded in 1995 following the dissolution of the Finnish Rural Party.
In which country is Interpol based?
Interpol: France. It is the world's largest international police organization.
Which of these was an official language of the Novgorod Republic?
Novgorod Republic: Old East Slavic. For much of its history, Novgorod was the center of Russian art and culture.
Which of these was an official language of Sheba?
Sheba: Sabaean. Sheba, or Saba, was an ancient South Arabian kingdom that existed in Yemen before 275 CE.
Which of these was an official language of the Kingdom of Jerusalem?
Kingdom of Jerusalem: Latin. The Kingdom of Jerusalem, also known as the Crusader Kingdom, was one of the Crusader states established in the Levant immediately after the First Crusade.
Of which country was Sanskrit an official language?

Sanskrit is an official language of Gupta Empire. The Gupta Empire was an Indian empire during the classical period of the Indian subcontinent which existed from the mid 3rd century to mid 6th century CE.
The son of a Trojan prince and the goddess Aphrodite, this mythological hero appears only briefly in Homer's Iliad but receives an entire Roman epic devoted to his journey — who is he?
Aeneas (in-; Classical; from Ancient) was a Trojan hero in Greco-Roman mythology, the son of the Trojan prince Anchises and the Greek goddess Aphrodite (equivalent to the Roman Venus).
She has led the AfD's parliamentary group in the Bundestag since 2017 and now co-chairs the party with Tino Chrupalla — which German politician is it?

Alice Weidel (born 6 February 1979) is a German far-right politician who has been serving as co-chairwoman of the far-right, vlkisch nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party alongside Tino Chrupalla since June 2022.
A career diplomat who advocated for the 2003 invasion of Iraq, this man went on to serve as the 71st U.S. secretary of state from 2021 to 2025 — who is he?
Antony Blinken (born April 16, 1962) is an American lawyer and diplomat who served as the 71st United States secretary of state from 2021 to 2025.

Originally depicted as a lioness, this ancient Egyptian goddess was later associated with the domestic cat and worshipped as early as 2890 BCE, sharing a dual nature with the warrior goddess Sekhmet — who is she?
Bastet (Ancient), also known as Ubasti or Bubastis, is a goddess of ancient Egyptian religion, possibly of Nubian origin, worshipped as early as the Second Dynasty (2890 BCE).
Believed to have once been an NKVD informant, this Polish communist led his country from 1948 to 1956 and imposed the Stalinist system there — who was he?
Bolesław Bierut (18 April 1892 - 12 March 1956) was a Polish communist activist and politician who was the leader of communist-ruled Poland from 1948 until 1956.

Eton-educated and aristocratic, this British general is best remembered for his 1781 surrender at Yorktown — yet he later governed both Ireland and India, where his name lives on in a famous legal code. Who was he?
Charles Cornwallis, 1st Marquess Cornwallis (31 December 1738 - 5 October 1805) was a British Army officer, Whig politician and colonial administrator.
This immensely wealthy final king of Lydia fell to Cyrus the Great after the fall of his capital, Sardis, in the 6th century BC — who was he?
Croesus (Ancient) was the last king of Lydia from 585 BC to 546 BC.
After a term as Russia's president, he swapped chairs to become prime minister from 2012 to 2020, and now serves as deputy chairman of the Security Council — which Russian politician is this?
Dmitry Medvedev (born 14 September 1965) is a Russian politician and lawyer who served as the president of Russia from 2008 to 2012 and as the prime minister of Russia from 2012 to 2020.
Dubbed the 'Father of the Nation' and also a noted historian behind the book Capitalism and Slavery, this leader steered Trinidad and Tobago to independence — who is it?
Eric Williams (25 September 1911 - 29 March 1981) was a Trinidad and Tobago politician.

This Dutch politician served as First Vice-President of the European Commission under Jean-Claude Juncker, later became the EU's climate action commissioner, and then led a Dutch political alliance in parliament from 2023 to 2025. Who is he?
Frans Timmermans (born 6 May 1961) is a Dutch politician who was the leader of GroenLinks-PvdA in the House of Representatives from 2023 to 2025.
Working alongside Simone de Beauvoir to expose torture during the Algerian War, this feminist lawyer later signed a landmark 1971 declaration demanding free abortion access — who is she?
Gisèle Halimi (born Zeiza Gisle lise Taeb,; 27 July 1927 - 28 July 2020) was a Tunisian-French lawyer, politician, essayist and feminist activist.
As China's top leader on Hong Kong and Macau affairs, this former Shanghai mayor rose to the Politburo Standing Committee before becoming vice president in 2023 — who is he?
Han Zheng (pinyin: Hn Zhng; born April 1955) is a Chinese politician who, since 2023, has served as the 11th vice president of China.
Dated to begin about 5,200 years ago with the invention of writing, this scholarly record traces humanity's religious feelings, thoughts, and ideas across the millennia — what field of study is this?
History of religion is the written record of human religious feelings, thoughts, and ideas.
A professor of Ukrainian language and a nationalist member of parliament from 2012 to 2014, this linguist campaigned hard for heritage-language learning - who is she?
Iryna Farion (29 April 1964 - 19 July 2024) was a Ukrainian linguist and nationalist politician who served as a deputy in the Verkhovna Rada from 2012 to 2014.

Elected New York's first female county judge and later county district attorney, this Lebanese-American TV host and lawyer has served as the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia since May 2025. Who is she?
Jeanine Pirro (born June 2, 1951) is a Lebanese-American television host, lawyer, and author who has been serving as the United States attorney for the District of Columbia since May 2025.
This Nova Scotian-born seaman turned his record-setting solo voyage aboard the Spray into the best-seller "Sailing Alone Around the World" — who was he?
Joshua Slocum (February 20, 1844 - on or shortly after November 14, 1909) was the first person to sail single-handedly around the world.
Commander of the Tobruk-based Libyan National Army, this officer has been the de facto ruler of eastern Libya since 2017, governing it as a military dictatorship. Who is he?
Khalifa Haftar (born 7 November 1943) is a Libyan politician, military officer, and the commander of the Tobruk-based Libyan National Army (LNA).
Born Lev Bronstein, this Marxist theorist stood with Lenin as one of the two most prominent figures of the early Soviet state — until he was exiled in 1929 and assassinated in 1940. Who was he?
Leon Trotsky was Soviet politician and revolutionary (1879–1940).
Chancellor of a university in Haryana and MLA for Tijara in Rajasthan, this politician also serves as the eighth head of a Hindu monastic sect — who is he?
Mahant Balaknath (born 16 April 1984) is an Indian politician and current MLA from Tijara constituency in Rajasthan.
This French politician has led the La France Insoumise parliamentary group in the National Assembly since 2021, having represented a Val-de-Marne constituency since 2017 — who is she?
Mathilde Panot (French; born 15 January 1989) is a French politician who has served as the president of the La France Insoumise group in the National Assembly since October 2021.
This Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare shared the Capitoline Triad with Jupiter and Juno, and is often shown with an owl — who is she?
Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom, justice, law, victory, and the sponsor of arts, trade, and strategy.
While 'nudism' stresses the practice itself, this near-synonym highlights an attitude of harmony with nature woven into non-sexual social nudity — which term?
Naturism is a lifestyle of practicing non-sexual social nudity in private and in public; the word also refers to the cultural movement which advocates and defends that lifestyle.
Marked by financial and personal failure before 1640, this English soldier rose to lead Parliament's army, championed the execution of Charles I, and ruled as Lord Protector. Who is he?
Oliver Cromwell (25 April 1599 - 3 September 1658) was an English statesman, farmer and soldier, widely regarded as one of the most important figures in British history.
This historical region in southwestern Iran, corresponding to Fars province, saw Iranic-speaking migrants arrive from Central Asia in ancient times — what is it called?
Persis is a historical region in south-western Iran, roughly corresponding with Fars province.

Officially known as the Religious Society of Friends, members of this Christian movement got their popular nickname after founder George Fox told a judge to 'quake before the authority of God' — what are they called?
Quakers are people who belong to the Religious Society of Friends, originally known as simply the Society of Friends, a historically Protestant Christian set of denominations.
A decorated Vietnam Marine awarded a Bronze Star and Purple Heart, he led the FBI as its sixth director from 2001 to 2013 after appointments under presidents of both parties. Who?
Robert Mueller (August 7, 1944 - March 20, 2026) was an American lawyer who served as the sixth director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) from 2001 to 2013.

Widely expected to succeed his mother as India's prime minister, this politician's sudden death in a 1980 plane crash instead paved the way for his older brother to inherit that political legacy — who was he?
Sanjay Gandhi (14 December 1946 - 23 June 1980) was an Indian politician.

This Yugoslav and Serbian politician served as president of Serbia (1989–1997) and then the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (1997–2000). He was the first sitting head of state charged with war crimes. Who is he?

Slobodan Milošević (Serbian) was a Yugoslav and Serbian politician who was the president of Serbia between 1989 and 1997 and president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1997 until his overthrow in 2000.
With an unclassified script of just 97 known inscriptions, this Bronze Age Iberian culture is considered the first named kingdom of southwestern Spain — which civilization?
Tartessos is, as defined by archaeological discoveries, a historical civilization settled in the southern Iberian Peninsula from about the late Bronze Age until the 5th century BC.

Led by Gamal Abdel Nasser, this short-lived political union between Egypt and Syria existed from 1958 until Syria seceded following a 1961 coup, with Egypt keeping the joint name until 1971 — what was this country called?
United Arab Republic was a country and sovereign state in the Middle East from 1958 to 1971.
After forcing the last Qing emperor's abdication and later dying in 1916, Yuan Shikai left behind a power vacuum that split China among competing military strongmen — which turbulent period followed?

Warlord Era was the period in the history of the Republic of China between 1916 and 1928, when control of the country was divided between rival military cliques of the Beiyang Army and other regional factions.

A longtime Communist Party member and labour lawyer, this Spanish politician founded an electoral alliance in 2023 while serving as her country's Minister of Labour and Second Deputy Prime Minister — who is she?

Yolanda Díaz (born 6 May 1971) is a Spanish politician and labour lawyer, currently serving as Second Deputy Prime Minister since 2021, and Minister of Labour and Social Economy of the Government of Spain since 2020.
Serving briefly as prime minister before becoming Turkey's president from 2007 to 2014, he earlier joined forces with a fellow reformist named Erdoğan after his party split in 2000 — who is he?
Abdullah Gül: President of Turkey from 2007 to 2014. Abdullah Gül (born 29 October 1950) is a Turkish politician who served as the president of Turkey from 2007 to 2014.
Crowned at just 13 under the regent Bairam Khan, this third Mughal emperor expanded the empire across much of the subcontinent and pursued a policy of conciliating those he conquered — who was he?
A barrister and journalist elected to Victoria's parliament at just 23, this 'father of Federation' went on to serve three separate terms as Australia's second prime minister — who is it?
Alfred Deakin: Prime Minister of Australia (1903–1904; 1905–1908; 1909–1910)

A Royal Navy helicopter pilot during the Falklands War and third child of Queen Elizabeth II, this former Duke of York married Sarah Ferguson in 1986 and stepped back from public roles amid scandal. Who is he?
Born on Delos as the twin sister of Apollo, this Greek goddess presided over hunting, wild animals, and childbirth while herself remaining chaste — who is she?
Artemis: Ancient Greek goddess. In one account, Artemis is born first and then proceeds to assist Leto in the birth of the second twin, Apollo.
This Thai princess, a practicing attorney, helped the United Nations craft the 'Bangkok Rules' on the treatment of incarcerated women — who was she?
Orphaned as a child and later working as a domestic servant, this Zapotec leader became Mexico's first Indigenous president and led the Liberals through the Reform War — who is he?
Benito Juárez: President of Mexico from 1858 to 1872.
A former construction worker who rose through Communist Party ranks before turning political independent, this Russian leader served as president from 1991 to 1999 — who was he?

Boris Yeltsin: President of Russia from 1991 to 1999. Boris Nikolayevich Yeltsin (1 February 1931 – 23 April 2007) was a Soviet and Russian politician who served as President of Russia from 1991 to 1999.
This Warsaw-born nobleman fought against foreign domination of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth before crossing the Atlantic to earn the title "The Father of American cavalry" — who was he?
Casimir Pulaski: Polish nobleman and American Revolutionary War general (1745–1779)
This Republican served as the 55th governor of New Jersey and later ran for his party's presidential nomination in both 2016 and 2024 — who is he?
Chris Christie: Governor of New Jersey from 2010 to 2018.

Emerging in Western Europe and the US during the Industrial Revolution, this socio-cultural phenomenon turns the acquisition of goods into something that shapes identity, not just meets basic needs — which term?
Consumerism: Acquisition of goods beyond essential needs.
A youngest son raised partly at the English court of Henry I, this 12th-century ruler and saint took the throne of Alba after his brother Alexander died in 1124 — who was he?
David I of Scotland: King of Alba from 1124 to 1153.
Nicknamed 'Da Vinci,' this Ukrainian commander became the youngest battalion leader in his country's army before being killed at the Battle of Bakhmut in 2023 — who was he?
The son of Alfred the Great, this king defeated a cousin's rival claim to secure the throne of the Anglo-Saxons in 899 — who is he?
Edward the Elder: King of the Anglo-Saxons from 899 to 924.
This Indonesian businessman-turned-politician once owned Italian football giant Inter Milan and now chairs his country's football federation — who is he?
Erick Thohir: Indonesian politician and businessman (born 1970)

This Portuguese explorer led the 1519 Spanish expedition that first crossed the Pacific and made European contact with the Philippines — where he was killed before his crew completed history's first circumnavigation. Who was he?
Closely tied to moral responsibility, praise, and blame, this philosophical capacity to choose one's own actions is debated over whether it can coexist with physical determinism — what is it called?
Free will: Ability to make choices voluntarily.
Known to his family as "Bertie," he was the last Emperor of India and became the first Head of the Commonwealth after the 1949 London Declaration — which king?
George VI: King of the United Kingdom from 1936 to 1952.
Serving as Texas's attorney general before becoming its governor in 2015, this Republican is now the longest-serving incumbent governor in the United States — who is he?

Greg Abbott: Governor of Texas since 2015. Gregory Wayne Abbott ( ABB-ət; born November 13, 1957) is an American politician, attorney, and jurist who has served since 2015 as the 48th governor of Texas.
Growing out of Lübeck in the late 12th century, which medieval trading network eventually spanned nearly 200 towns from Estonia to the Netherlands?
Hanseatic League: 1200s–1669 trade confederation in Northern Europe.
Also known as the White Huns, this Central Asian people defeated the Kidarites in 450 CE before falling to a joint Turkic-Sasanian force in 560 — who were they?
Hephthalites: 5th–8th-century nomadic confederation in Central Asia.
Adopted in 1917 to shed a German-sounding surname amid wartime sentiment, this royal lineage has included five monarchs, from George V to Charles III — which royal family?
House of Windsor: British royal family. The House of Windsor is the current royal house of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms.
Known to the Akkadians as Ishtar and symbolized by a lion and an eight-pointed star, which Mesopotamian goddess of war and love was worshipped at a temple in Uruk?
Inanna: Ancient Mesopotamian goddess. Inanna was worshipped in Sumer as early as the Uruk period (c. 4000 – 3100 BCE), and her worship was relatively localized before the conquest of Sargon of Akkad.
A last-minute swap onto the Apollo 13 crew, this command module pilot rode the famous aborted mission farther from Earth than any astronaut would travel for decades — who was he?
Jack Swigert: American astronaut and politician (1931–1982)

Sister of a president, two U.S. senators, and the founder of the Special Olympics, this diplomat served as U.S. Ambassador to Ireland and convinced Bill Clinton to grant a controversial visa to a Sinn Féin leader — who is she?
Nicknamed 'Black Jack,' this general commanded the American Expeditionary Forces in World War I and mentored future leaders like Eisenhower, Patton, and MacArthur — who is he?
John J. Pershing: United States Army general (1860–1948)
A French naval officer and botanist, he explored the Pacific, New Zealand and Antarctica — and as a cartographer left his name on seaweeds, plants, and an island. Who is it?
Jules Dumont d'Urville: French explorer and naval officer (1790–1842)
Nicknamed "The Conqueror," this King of Dál Riada subdued the Picts in the 840s and moved the Stone of Scone to his new capital at Forteviot — who was he?
Kenneth MacAlpin: King of the Picts from 848 to 858.
Ruling the Vijayanagara Empire at its political and cultural peak from 1509 to 1529, this emperor defeated the sultans of Bijapur and Golconda and conquered the Raichur Doab in 1512 — who was he?

Krishnadevaraya: Emperor of Vijayanagara from 1509 to 1529. Krishnadevaraya (17 January 1471 – 17 October 1529) was emperor of the Vijayanagara Empire from 1509 to 1529 and the third ruler of the Tuluva dynasty.
This Argentine general seized the presidency by ousting his predecessor in 1981, backed the Contras in Nicaragua, and continued the military junta's 'Dirty War' — who is he?
Leopoldo Galtieri: Argentine general and military ruler (1926–2003)
Legend credits this man with toppling Rome's last king after the suicide of Lucretia and becoming one of the Republic's first two consuls — who was he?
Lucius Junius Brutus: Semi-legendary 6th-century BC founder of Roman Republic.
Serving in the Karnataka Legislative Assembly for over three decades, this Indian politician has led the Indian National Congress as president since 2022 — who is he?
Mallikarjun Kharge: Indian lawyer and politician (born 1942)
Elected to the Chamber of Deputies in the 2018 Italian general election, this politician represents the Forza Italia party — who is she?

Named after a 16th-century Frisian cleric, this Anabaptist Christian movement traces to the Radical Reformation and later codified beliefs like adult baptism and foot washing in its 1632 Dordrecht Confession — what is it called?
Mennonites: Anabaptist groups originating in Western Europe.
Ruler of the Kingdom of Pontus in northern Anatolia, this king waged repeated but unsuccessful wars against Rome for dominance over Asia Minor and the Black Sea — who was he?
Mithridates VI Eupator: King of Pontus from 120 to 63 BC.
During this Ottoman sultan's reign Morocco briefly became a vassal before breaking free, and ties with Elizabethan England were forged over a shared enemy; who was this 16th-century ruler?
Murad III: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1574 to 1595.
Born into a prominent Catholic mandarin family, he became South Vietnam's first president in 1955 and ruled until his assassination during a CIA-backed coup in 1963 — who was he?

Ngo Dinh Diem: President of South Vietnam from 1955 to 1963. Diệm was born into a prominent Catholic family with his father, Ngô Đình Khả, being a high-ranking mandarin for Emperor Thành Thái during the French colonial era.
Succeeding his kinsman as ruler of Novgorod, this Varangian prince extended control along the Dnieper to Kiev and led a successful raid on Constantinople before his death in 912 — who was he?
Oleg the Wise: Varangian prince, founder of Kievan Rus'
The eldest daughter of a former president, she became the first woman elected head of state in South Korea — and in all of East Asia — before being removed from office in 2017. Who is she?

Park Geun-hye: President of South Korea from 2013 to 2017. Park previously served as the acting first lady of South Korea under her father's presidency from 1974 until her father's assassination in 1979.

Its name comes from Ancient Greek for "love of wisdom," and once upon a time physics and psychology were considered branches of it before going their separate academic ways. What rational, critical field is this?
Philosophy: Study of general and fundamental questions.

Nicknamed 'the Flautist' for his love of playing the flute at Dionysian festivals, this Macedonian-Greek king ruled Egypt twice and was a descendant of one of Alexander the Great's generals — who was he?
Ptolemy XII Auletes: Ptolemaic King of Egypt, 80–51 BC.

Turkish politician who rose from Istanbul mayor to prime minister (2003–2014) and has been president since 2014, co-founding the AKP. His rule has drawn criticism for democratic backsliding. Who is he?
Recep Tayyip Erdoğan: President of Turkey since 2014. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (born 26 February 1954) is a Turkish politician and statesman who has been the president of Turkey since 2014.
The first person to walk to both the North and South Poles, this explorer later led his son on a 600-mile renewable-energy-only trek to the South Pole in 2017 — who is he?
The oldest daughter of her husband's own uncle, this woman was the wife of former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein and mother to sons Uday and Qusay — who is she?
Sajida Talfah: First wife of Saddam Hussein.
This 44-day conflict in 2020 ended in an Azerbaijani victory over Armenia and the breakaway state of Artsakh, with the defeat sparking anti-government protests in Yerevan — what was it?
Second Nagorno-Karabakh War: Conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan (2020)
The first Iranian ever to win the Nobel Peace Prize, this lawyer and former judge was honored in 2003 for her work on democracy and women's, children's and refugee rights — who is she?

Held every March in Austin, Texas, since 1987, this tech-film-music extravaganza also spun off an EDU conference and a London edition — what's this festival, often shortened to a three-letter abbreviation?
South by Southwest: American annual film and music festival.
Born to a Cossack family in Poltava, this journalist-turned-revolutionary became Supreme Commander of the Ukrainian People's Army during the Ukrainian War of Independence — who was he?
Serving as Dachau's second commandant and later the first inspector of Nazi concentration camps, this SS commander was killed in 1943 when his plane was shot down over Kharkov — who was he?
Grand Duke Konstantin Pavlovich of Russia
This Japanese term describes marginalized, often homeless youth — a mix of runaways and those seeking community after bullying — who gather in Kabukicho's back alleys. What is this subculture called?
Toyoko kids: Youth group in Tokyo, Japan.
Born in Jaffna, this guerrilla leader founded and led a militant organization in a decades-long campaign for an independent Tamil state in Sri Lanka — who is he?
Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine
Velupillai Prabhakaran: Leader of militant Tamil organisation in Sri Lanka (1954–2009)
This Chinese diplomat served as ambassador to Japan before becoming Minister of Foreign Affairs and later director of the Communist Party's Central Foreign Affairs Commission Office — who is he?
Alongside Andrew Moray, this Scottish knight won the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297 before being captured and executed for treason in 1305 — who is he?
William Wallace: Scottish knight (1270–1305). Along with Andrew Moray, Wallace defeated an English army at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in September 1297.

Born to a family of strawberry farmers in Akita Prefecture, this politician rose to become Japan's Prime Minister from 2020 to 2021 after years as Chief Cabinet Secretary under Shinzo Abe — who is he?

Yoshihide Suga: Prime Minister of Japan from 2020 to 2021. Yoshihide Suga (菅 義偉, Suga Yoshihide; born 6 December 1948) is a Japanese former politician who served as Prime Minister of Japan from 2020 to 2021.

Henrietta Swan Leavitt (born 1868) is the earliest of the four. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (July 4, 1868 – December 12, 1921) was an American astronomer.
Which one below was born first?
Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Who among these was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four came first?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Toghon Temür is an astronomer. Toghon Temür acceded to the throne in 1333 after years of succession disputes following his father's death.
Who among these is a mathematician?
John Horton Conway is a mathematician. John Horton Conway (26 December 1937 – 11 April 2020) was an English mathematician.
What is the atomic number of Caesium?
Caesium (IUPAC spelling; also spelled cesium in American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Cs and atomic number 55.
What is the atomic number of Tungsten?
Tungsten (also called wolfram) is a chemical element; it has symbol W (from German: Wolfram) and atomic number 74.
In what year did Hamish Harding die?
Hamish Harding: George Hamish Livingston Harding (24 June 1964 – 18 June 2023) was a British businessman, pilot and adventurer based in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
In what year was Pluto discovered?
Pluto (minor-planet number 134340) is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
TypeScript: Anders Hejlsberg. TypeScript (TS) is a high-level programming language that adds static typing with optional type annotations to JavaScript.
Pethidine: Pfizer. Pethidine, also known as meperidine and sold under the brand name Demerol among others, is a fully synthetic opioid pain medication of the phenylpiperidine class.
Who is credited with discovering Archaeopteryx?
Archaeopteryx: Carl Friedrich Häberlein. Archaeopteryx (lit. 'ancient wing'), sometimes referred to by its German name, "Urvogel " (lit. 'Primeval Bird') is an extinct genus of bird-like dinosaurs.
Who is credited with discovering Oganesson?
Oganesson: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
Who is credited with discovering Cimetidine?
Cimetidine: John Colin Emmett. Cimetidine, sold under the brand name Tagamet among others, is a histamine H2 receptor antagonist that inhibits stomach acid production.
Who is credited with discovering Iridium?
Iridium: Smithson Tennant. Iridium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ir and atomic number 77.
A broad-spectrum benzimidazole drug, this medicine clears intestinal parasites from pinworm to hookworm to tapeworm — which agent is it?
Albendazole is a broad-spectrum antihelmintic and antiprotozoal agent of the benzimidazole type.
A balloon-like bulge at a weakened patch of vessel wall, it can turn lethal in the brain's circle of Willis or the aorta if it bursts — what is this?
Aneurysm is an outward bulging, likened to a bubble or balloon, caused by a localized, abnormal, weak spot on a blood vessel wall.
Founder of a prominent Russian design studio and an avid, famously foul-mouthed blogger, this designer and entrepreneur is also a member of the Tolstoy family — name this designer?
Artemy Lebedev (born 13 February 1975) is a Russian designer, entrepreneur and Internet personality.
Built under license from the Swiss Pilatus PC-9, this turboprop trainer serves the US Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps and flies in Canada under the designation CT-156 Harvard — which aircraft?
Beechcraft T-6 Texan II is a single-engined, turboprop aircraft currently built by Textron Aviation, formerly manufactured by Raytheon Aircraft Company, which sold to Textron in 2007.
Born as Hughes Helicopters' Model 77 to replace the AH-1 Cobra, this twin-turboshaft attack helicopter packs a 30 mm chain gun and Hellfire missiles in a tandem cockpit — what is it?
Boeing AH-64 Apache (-) is an American twin-turboshaft attack helicopter with a tailwheel-type landing gear and a tandem cockpit for a crew of two.

Synthesized by the liver in response to inflammation, this ring-shaped blood molecule binds to the surface of dead or dying cells to activate the immune system's complement cascade. What is it commonly called?
C-reactive protein (CRP) is an annular (ring-shaped) pentameric protein found in blood plasma, whose circulating concentration rises in response to inflammation.
Which metabolic process is the polar opposite of anabolism, breaking large molecules such as proteins and lipids down into monomers while releasing energy, some of it lost as heat?
Catabolism is the set of metabolic pathways that breaks down molecules into smaller units that are either oxidized to release energy or used in other anabolic reactions.
Linked to repeated head trauma, this worsening neurodegenerative disease turns up in boxers and footballers — and even in soccer players, largely from heading the ball. What is it?

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative disease linked to repeated trauma to the head. The encephalopathy symptoms can include behavioral problems, mood problems, and problems with thinking.
This highly poisonous member of the carrot family can grow to nearly 8 feet tall, with hollow, maroon-spotted stems and a famously unpleasant odor — what plant is it?
Conium maculatum (British English) or poison hemlock (in North America), is a highly poisonous flowering plant and a nitrophile weed species in the carrot family Apiaceae.
Nearly every genus in this taxonomic family of armadillos is extinct, except for one genus that still includes eight living species today. Name the family?
Dasypodidae is a family of mostly extinct genera of armadillos.
What flying insect, of which about 3,000 species exist, is known for its large compound eyes, two pairs of transparent wings, and often iridescent, metallic body coloration?
Dragonfly is a flying insect belonging to the infraorder Anisoptera below the order Odonata.
This discipline systematically applies natural science and mathematics to design solutions like bridges, pacemakers, and spacecraft under real-world constraints. What field is it?
Engineering is the practice of systematically applying natural science and mathematics to design and improve systems, devices, or processes that solve problems under constraints.
Colloquially called 'squirting,' this phenomenon involves fluid from the Skene's gland and is physiologically distinct from coital incontinence — what is it?
Female ejaculation is characterized as an expulsion of fluid from the Skene's gland at the lower end of the urethra during or before an orgasm.
This American video game businessman dropped out of Harvard to join Microsoft, where he worked on early Windows and a Doom port, before co-founding Valve Corporation in 1996 — who is he?
Gabe Newell (born November 3, 1962), also known by his nickname GabeN, is an American video game developer and businessman.
Comprising about 50 species native to tropical regions worldwide, this genus produces roughly 80% of the world's natural fiber and doubles as an oilseed crop — which genus?
Gossypium is a genus of flowering plants in the tribe Gossypieae of the mallow family, Malvaceae, from which cotton is harvested.

One of the first plants ever spun into fiber some 50,000 years ago, which fast-growing Cannabis sativa cultivar is grown for rope, textiles, paper, biofuel and food rather than its psychoactive punch?
Hemp is a plant in the botanical class of Cannabis sativa cultivars grown specifically for industrial and consumable use.

This large insect order includes sawflies, wasps, bees, and ants, with more than 150,000 described species, many of whose females have an egg-laying organ often modified into a stinger — what is it called?
Hymenoptera is a large order of insects, comprising the sawflies, wasps, bees, and ants.
This mild oxidizing agent and Lewis acid, with the formula FeCl3, is commonly used to purify water and to etch metal surfaces — which compound is it?
Iron(III) chloride is an inorganic compound with the formula FeCl3. The anhydrous derivative is a Lewis acid, while all forms are mild oxidizing agents.
This Confederate veteran and pharmacist sold the rights to his 1886 beverage recipe to Asa Griggs Candler for about $2,300 shortly before he died — who is he?
John Stith Pemberton (July 8, 1831 - August 16, 1888) was an American pharmacist, chemist, and Confederate States Army officer who is best known as the inventor of Coca-Cola.
Originally a water-retrieving gun dog from Italy's Po Delta marshes, this breed later became prized for hunting truffles once its wetland habitat was drained — what breed is it?
Lagotto Romagnolo is an Italian breed of dog.
Named after a pioneer of sterile surgery, this genus of rod-shaped bacteria can multiply even at refrigerator temperatures and causes a rare but serious foodborne illness — what is it?
Listeria is a genus of bacteria that acts as an intracellular parasite in mammals.
Formed from two glucose units linked by an alpha(1→4) bond, which disaccharide, a reducing sugar unlike sucrose, is released when starch breaks down during malting?
Maltose (or), also known as maltobiose or malt sugar, is a disaccharide formed from two units of glucose joined with an (14) bond.
More than 80% of cases trace to asbestos exposure, and it grows from the thin lining covering the lungs and other organs — which cancer is it?
Mesothelioma is a type of cancer that develops from the thin layer of tissue that covers many of the internal organs (known as the mesothelium).
This genus of edible sac fungi has a honeycomb-like cap of ridges and pits, is prized in French and Catalan cooking, and turns toxic if eaten raw or undercooked. What fungus is this?
Morchella is a genus of edible sac fungi closely related to anatomically simpler cup fungi in the order Pezizales (division Ascomycota).

Encompassing three distinct genetic conditions marked by nervous-system tumors, one type brings café au lait skin spots and scoliosis while another causes early-onset hearing loss and cataracts — which condition?
Neurofibromatosis (NF) refers to a group of three distinct genetic conditions in which tumors grow in the nervous system.
Which applied-math discipline, born from pre-WWII military planning and overlapping heavily with industrial engineering, hunts for the maximum profit or minimum cost in real-world problems?

Operations research (British), often shortened to the initialism OR, is a branch of applied mathematics that deals with the development and application of analytical methods to improve management and decision-making.
This Scottish biologist-turned-town-planner coined the word 'conurbation' and his work contains one of the earliest versions of 'think globally, act locally.' Who was he?
Patrick Geddes (2 October 1854 - 17 April 1932) was a Scottish biologist, sociologist, Comtean positivist, geographer, philanthropist and pioneering town planner.
This genus of spiders in the family Ctenidae is found mainly in northern South America, with a single species ranging into Central America — name this genus?
Phoneutria is a genus of spiders in the family Ctenidae.

Native to most of the Northern Hemisphere, this genus of 25 to 30 deciduous tree species includes poplars, aspens, and cottonwoods, one of which was the first tree ever fully DNA-sequenced — which genus?
Populus is a genus of 25-30 species of deciduous flowering plants in the family Salicaceae, native to most of the Northern Hemisphere.
This yellow-white fluid forms at sites of infection and inflammation — when trapped in tissue it's called an abscess, and near the skin's surface a pimple — name the substance?
Pus is an exudate, typically white-yellow, yellow, or yellow-brown, formed at the site of inflammation during infections, regardless of cause.
Also known as vitamin B2, this nutrient builds two key coenzymes for energy metabolism and may, taken orally, cut down on migraine headaches in adults — what is it?
Riboflavin is a vitamin found in food and sold as a dietary supplement.
Having coded his first game in high school and studied computer science in Tokyo, this man went on to lead Nintendo by championing fun over raw horsepower — who is he?
Satoru Iwata (December 6, 1959 - July 11, 2015) was a Japanese businessman, video game programmer and producer.
Element number 14 is a tetravalent non-metal sometimes called a metalloid, prized for the transistors and integrated circuits it makes possible — which one is it?
Silicon is a chemical element; it has symbol Si and atomic number 14.
A self-taught Indian genius of infinite series and number theory, he initially struggled to interest established mathematicians because his methods were so unfamiliar — who was he?
Srinivasa Ramanujan (22 December 1887 - 26 April 1920) was an Indian mathematician who worked during the early 20th century.
Deriving its name from a French word for crushed oak bark used in hide-curing, this class of astringent plant compounds binds to and precipitates proteins and other organic molecules — what is it?
Tannin (or tannoids) are a class of astringent, polyphenolic biomolecules that bind to and precipitate proteins and various other organic compounds including amino acids and alkaloids.
This genus of about 30 tree and shrub species is native across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, with its greatest diversity found in Asia — what genus is it?
Tilia is a genus of about 30 species of trees or bushes, native throughout most of the temperate Northern Hemisphere.
What is the medical term for having dangerously high levels of urea in the blood, typically caused by kidney failure?

Uremia is the condition of having high levels of urea in the blood. It is the signs, symptoms and results from laboratory tests which result from inadequate excretory, regulatory, and endocrine function of the kidneys.
These big cetaceans — everything in the group except dolphins and porpoises — count the hippopotamus as their closest living relative on land. What are they?
Whale are a widely distributed and diverse group of fully aquatic placental marine mammals.
The only living member of its entire mammalian order, this nocturnal African burrower uses its long snout and powerful claws to dig ants and termites out of their mounds — what animal is it?
Aardvark: Burrowing mammal native to Africa.
While bacteria and some plants may be biologically immortal, this universal process in humans slows reaction time even as knowledge tends to grow — what is it called?
Ageing: Biological process of getting older.
This genus of over 650 succulent species includes a 'true' member long used in pharmaceutical products, native to Africa, Madagascar, and the Arabian Peninsula — which genus?
Aloe: Genus of succulent flowering plants.
Struck off the medical register for 'serious professional misconduct,' this former surgeon authored the fraudulent 1998 Lancet paper falsely tying the MMR vaccine to autism — who is he?

Latin for 'worm-shaped,' this finger-like, blind-ended tube branches off the cecum and, though long considered vestigial, may actually serve as a reservoir for beneficial gut bacteria. What structure is this?
Appendix (anatomy): Tube attached to the intestine.
This ocean giant, recorded at up to 680 kg, has vanished from the Black Sea but still roams the Mediterranean and both sides of another major ocean — which fish?
Atlantic bluefin tuna: Species of fish. The Atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus) is a species of tuna in the family Scombridae.

Members of the family Ursidae walk flat on plantigrade paws tipped with five claws that can't retract — and though most eat meat, the giant panda among them is mostly herbivorous. What animal is this?
Made by combining phenol and acetone, this compound forms 65 to 70 percent of the world's polycarbonate plastics production — which chemical?
Bisphenol A: Chemical used in plastics, xenoestrogen.
Formerly called the Russian Wolfhound until 1936, this Russian sighthound breed was originally used for hunting wolves. What breed is it?
Named after the Greek word for butter via butyric acid, this colorless, highly flammable gas exists as two isomers and vaporizes quickly at room temperature — what alkane is it?
Native to Africa, the Middle East, and arid parts of Asia, this nocturnal, secretive wild cat is built for the chase with long legs and dramatically long tufted ears — which animal?
Also called bachelor's button, this European annual once grew as a common weed among grain fields but is now endangered there due to herbicides — what flower is it?
Centaurea cyanus: Species of flowering plant.

Nicknamed for its spider-like look and also called airplane plant or hen and chicks, this houseplant is native to tropical Africa but can suffer 'burnt tips' from fluoride in tap water — which species?
Chlorophytum comosum: Species of flowering plant. It is native to tropical and Southern Africa but has become naturalized in other parts of the world, including Western Australia and Bangladesh.
A shrub-like bush of western South America with oval leaves and small red berries, its leaves are chewed or brewed as a mild stimulant and famously contain a notorious alkaloid — which plant is it?
Coca: Plant in the Erythroxylaceae family.
This miniature Belgian-French dog breed comes in two varieties named for a butterfly and a moth, based on whether their ears stand erect or hang down — which breed?
Continental Toy Spaniel: Belgian and French breed of dog. The Épagneul Nain Continental or Continental Toy Spaniel is a Belgian and French breed of dog of spaniel type and of miniature or toy size.
First flown in 1938 and built almost 14,000 strong at a factory in Buffalo, New York, this WWII fighter-bomber was known to British and Soviet pilots as the Tomahawk or Kittyhawk — which aircraft?
Curtiss P-40 Warhawk: American WWII fighter. The Curtiss P-40 Warhawk is an American single-engined, single-seat, all-metal fighter-bomber that first flew in 1938.

Known mainly through DNA evidence rather than plentiful fossils, this extinct archaic human group ranged across Asia until about 32,000 years ago, and DNA analysis confirmed the Harbin skull belonged to it — what group is it?
Denisovan: Archaic human species from Asia.
In 1949, this NASA mathematician became the first African-American woman to supervise a team at Langley, later teaching herself and her staff the Fortran language — who is she?
Dorothy Vaughan: American human computer and computer programmer (1910–2008)
Linked with orgasm and involving involuntary pelvic-floor contractions, this male bodily process can even happen during sleep as a so-called 'wet dream' — what is it?
Ejaculation: Semen discharge from the male reproductive tract.
This 1939 Nobel Physics laureate invented the cyclotron and went on to found two national laboratories that carry his surname today — who was he?

Scientifically known as Chloris chloris, this small finch is widespread across Europe, North Africa, and Southwest Asia, and has also been introduced to Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay, and Argentina — what bird is this?
European greenfinch: Species of bird. The European greenfinch or simply the greenfinch (Chloris chloris) is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae.
Historically used in the 18th century to track down escaped slaves, this large Brazilian dog breed of mastiff type now also serves as a guard dog and companion — which breed?
Fila Brasileiro: Brazilian breed of dog. The Fila Brasileiro (Portuguese pronunciation: [ˈfilɐ bɾaziˈlejɾu]) is a Brazilian breed of large working dog of mastiff type.

Coated in cornmeal and pan-cooked while still unripe, this dish was originally a Northeastern and Midwestern staple before a hit movie rebranded it as quintessentially Southern comfort food — what is it?
Fried green tomatoes: American dish. Fried green tomatoes is a culinary dish usually found in the United States, made from unripe (green) tomatoes coated with cornmeal and fried.

Working at Tuskegee Institute, this agricultural scientist urged cotton farmers to plant peanuts and sweet potatoes instead, publishing dozens of practical bulletins to fight soil depletion. Who is he?
George Washington Carver: American botanist and inventor (1864–1943)
A U.S. Navy rear admiral who helped develop COBOL, this computer science pioneer wrote what's considered the first computer manual and worked on the Harvard Mark I — who is she?
Grace Hopper: U.S. naval officer and computer scientist (1906–1992)
Occurring in any of the senses, this perception feels completely real despite the absence of any actual external stimulus — what is it?
Hallucination: Perception that only seems real.
Some called egrets and others bitterns, these 75 species of long-legged, long-beaked wading birds make up the family Ardeidae — what are they?
Heron: Family of birds. The OED also observes that shiterow or shederow are terms used for herons, and also applied as derogatory terms meaning a thin, weakly person.
A colorless, flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor, this N2H4 compound foams polymer plastics, fills airbag gas generators, and serves as a storable spacecraft propellant. What is it?
Hydrazine: Colorless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor. It is a simple pnictogen hydride, and is a colourless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odour.
Powered by four Aviadvigatel turbofans and built in Voronezh, this Soviet-designed wide-body jet now serves mainly as the Russian president's aircraft — which airliner?
Ilyushin Il-96: Russian four-engined long-range wide-body jet airliner.

This Scottish physicist's equations unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single theory — the second great unification in physics after Newton's — while also helping found statistical mechanics — who is he?
James Clerk Maxwell: Scottish physicist and mathematician (1831–1879)
Struggling with a morphine addiction from a Civil War saber wound, this pharmacist and chemist developed a coca-and-caffeine beverage in 1886 that became Coca-Cola — who is he?
John Stith Pemberton: American pharmacist, inventor of Coca-Cola (1831–1888)
A pastor's son and theoretical physicist, this man passed Manhattan Project secrets to the Soviets, served nine years in a British prison, then resumed his science career in East Germany. Who is he?
Klaus Fuchs: German-born British physicist and atomic spy (1911–1988)
Formulated in 1834, this principle of electromagnetism states that an induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the very change in magnetic field that created it — which principle?
Lenz's law: Electromagnetic opposition to change.

Born from a 1970s Skunk Works project to dodge Soviet missile defenses, this subsonic single-seat attack jet became the first operational aircraft ever designed around stealth technology, first flying in 1981 at Groom Lake — which aircraft is it?
Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk: American stealth ground-attack aircraft.

Founder of the Kerala school, this Indian mathematician was the first to use infinite series to approximate trigonometric functions — a 'decisive step' toward the limit-passage to infinity; who is he?
Madhava of Sangamagrama: Indian mathematician and astronomer (1340–1425)
Growing out of calculus and the study of derivatives and integrals, this branch of mathematics examines functions, spaces, and limits using methods of approximation and convergence — which field?

Mathematical analysis: Branch of mathematics. Mathematical analysis is the branch of mathematics that studies functions, spaces, and operators through quantitative methods of approximation and convergence.
Sold under the brand name Dolophine, this synthetic opioid is used to manage chronic pain and treat opioid use disorder by relieving cravings and withdrawal. What is it?
Methadone: Opioid analgesic and maintenance therapy.

A hemiparasitic plant that taps into its host tree via a structure called the haustorium to steal water and nutrients, its European species was introduced to Northern California in 1900 — what plant is it?
Mistletoe: Common name for various parasitic plants.
Its Inuktitut name means 'the bearded one,' and males emit a strong odor during rut to attract mates — which thick-coated Arctic mammal is this?
Muskox: Species of arctic land mammal.
Popularized by neurologist George Beard in the 1860s, this diagnosis described fatigue, anxiety, and heart palpitations often blamed on the stresses of modern life — what was the condition called?
This condition of involuntary eye movement can be triggered by stimulating the ear's semicircular canals — for example with the caloric test — while the head stays still. What is it?
Nystagmus: Dysfunction of eye movement. Nystagmus is a condition of involuntary (or voluntary, in some cases) eye movement.
A playful, fish-eating cousin of weasels and badgers, this semiaquatic mammal is known for sliding down natural slides and toying with stones — what is it?
Also called androgenetic alopecia, this condition driven by male sex hormones and genetics shows up as a receding hairline or a thinning crown in men — what's the common name for it?
Pattern hair loss: Medical condition. Pattern hair loss, also known as androgenetic alopecia, is a hair loss condition that primarily affects the top and front of the scalp.
Sold under the brand name Luminal, this WHO-recommended barbiturate treats epilepsy in children and can be given intravenously for status epilepticus — which drug?
Phenobarbital: Medication of the barbiturate type.
Injected by a mosquito's bite and multiplying first in the liver before invading red blood cells, this parasite genus is the cause of malaria — what is it?
Plasmodium: Genus of parasitic protists that can cause malaria.
Originating in Spain's Canary Islands, this large mastiff-type breed was historically used for guarding, herding sheep and cattle, and — legally until 1936 — dog fighting. Which breed?
Presa Canario: Spanish breed of dog. It originates in the Spanish autonomous community of the Canary Islands, and is found mostly in the islands of Gran Canaria and Tenerife.
Usually caused by E. coli spreading up the urinary tract, this kidney infection typically brings fever and flank tenderness, and can be prevented by urinating after sex — what condition is it?
Pyelonephritis: Inflammation of the kidney. It is typically due to a bacterial infection, most commonly Escherichia coli.
From a startled jump to a cat automatically reorienting itself mid-fall, this involuntary, split-second reaction runs through the nervous system without needing conscious thought — what's it called?
Reflex: Automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus.
Commonly called the dog rose, this variable climbing wild plant is native to Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia — which species?
Also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type III, this rare genetic disorder is caused by the body's inability to break down certain sugar molecules called glycosaminoglycans — what is it called?

Sanfilippo syndrome: Rare metabolism disorder. Sanfilippo syndrome, also known as mucopolysaccharidosis type III (MPS III), is a rare lifelong genetic disease that mainly affects the brain and spinal cord.
Considered paradoxical by the ancient Greeks in Zeno's puzzle about motion, what term describes an infinite sum of terms added one after another, later made rigorous through the concept of a limit?
Series (mathematics): Infinite sum. In mathematics, a series is, roughly speaking, an addition of infinitely many terms, one after the other.
The sixth most abundant element in Earth's crust, this soft alkali metal carries symbol Na and pairs with chlorine as the ocean's most common dissolved element — what is it?
Sodium: Chemical element with atomic number 11 (Na)
Named in 1880 from Greek words meaning 'bunch of grapes,' this genus of spherical, grape-clustered bacteria can grow with or without oxygen — which genus?
Striking suddenly and resolving — one way or another — within 8 to 10 hours, this mysterious epidemic first hit England in 1485 and vanished after a final outbreak in 1551 — what was it called?
Sweating sickness: Contagious disease in Europe, 1485–1551.
An Australian-American math prodigy who won the Fields Medal in 2006, he proved a famous theorem on prime numbers with Ben Green in 2004. Who is he?
Terence Tao: Australian and American mathematician (born 1975)

Proposing an information-management system in March 1989, this English computer scientist implemented the first web browser and web server and founded the organization that still oversees the web's standards — who is he?

Endemic to New Zealand and often mistaken for a lizard, this reptile is the sole surviving member of an order that thrived back in the Mesozoic era — its Māori name means 'peaks on the back.' What is it?
Tuatara: Species of reptile. The tuatara (Māori: [ˈtʉ.a.ta.ɾa]; Sphenodon punctatus) is a species of reptile endemic to New Zealand.

Nicknamed the 'vampire fish' for feeding on the blood of larger fish through their gills, this tiny Amazonian catfish is infamous for an alleged, rare habit of entering human body openings — what is it?
Vandellia cirrhosa: Species of ray-finned fish.
Native to the Baltic, Black, and Caspian Sea basins, this large freshwater fish's range now stretches from the UK to western China — which species?
Wels catfish: Species of fish. It has been introduced to several countries in Western Europe, Mediterranean and Asia as a prized sport fish.
Ukraine's first female prime minister, she co-led the Orange Revolution and later led the Batkivshchyna party while championing EU integration — who is she?
Yulia Tymoshenko: Prime Minister of Ukraine (2005, 2007–2010)
What is the chemical symbol for lead?
The symbol for lead is Pb. Lead is a chemical element with the symbol Pb and atomic number 82.
The symbol for moscovium is Mc. Moscovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mc and atomic number 115.

In what year was Cher born?
Cher (SHAIR; legally mononymous; born Cheryl Sarkisian, May 20, 1946) is an American singer and actress.
In what year was Olga Kurylenko born?
Olga Kurylenko: Olga Kostyantynivna Kurylenko (born 14 November 1979) is a Ukrainian-born French actress and former model.
In what year was Gal Gadot born?
Gal Gadot (Hebrew: גל גדות, pronounced [ˈɡal ɡaˈdot]; born 30 April 1985) is an Israeli actress.
In what year was Lily-Rose Depp born?
Lily-Rose Depp: Lily-Rose Melody Depp (born May 27, 1999) is a French and American actress and singer.
In what year was Fran Drescher born?
Fran Drescher: Francine Joy Drescher (born September 30, 1957) is an American actress, writer, comedian, producer, and former trade union leader.
In what year was Chuck Norris born?
Chuck Norris: Carlos Ray "Chuck" Norris (March 10, 1940 – March 19, 2026) was an American martial artist, actor, screenwriter, and author.

Prabhas made his acting debut with the drama Eeswar (2002) and later attained his breakthrough with the action romance Varsham (2004).
In what year was George Lucas born?
George Lucas: George Walton Lucas Jr. (born May 14, 1944) is an American filmmaker and philanthropist.
In what year was Golshifteh Farahani born?
Golshifteh Farahani: Rahavard Farahani (Persian: رهاورد فراهانی; born 10 July 1983), known professionally as Golshifteh Farahani (گلشیفته فراهانی), is an Iranian actress.
In what year was Robert Redford born?
Robert Redford: Redford began his career on television in the late 1950s, appearing in anthology series such as Alfred Hitchcock Presents and The Twilight Zone.
In what year was James Caan born?
James Caan: James Edmund Caan ( KAHN; March 26, 1940 – July 6, 2022) was an American actor.
In what year did Roald Dahl die?
